The sympatry models (Step 2) show whether heterospecific songs are more or less different in sympatry, but a dyadic comparison cannot tell which species changed. Here we ask, for each focal species, whether populations that co-occur with a given congener are acoustically closer to (convergence) or farther from (divergence) that congener’s song than conspecific populations that do not co-occur with it.

title: Step 3: Population shifts towards or away from congeners
text:
Summary

Model summary

Only two of the twelve focal-congener combinations have enough data to test (populations with and without the congener, plus congener reference populations elsewhere): Ruficollis vs. Hypoxantha and the reverse, Hypoxantha vs. Ruficollis. Neither co-occurrence effect is credible (Ruficollis vs. Hypoxantha: -0.228 SD, 95% CI [-0.778, 0.405]; Hypoxantha vs. Ruficollis: 0.004 SD, 95% CI [-0.537, 0.554]).
The Hypoxantha vs. Ruficollis model shows a convergence warning (Rhat = 1.094) and a high divergent-transition rate (3128/20,000 draws, 15.6%), so its null result should be treated as inconclusive rather than as evidence of no shift. The Ruficollis vs. Hypoxantha model converged cleanly (Rhat = 1.003, 146/20,000 divergent, 0.7%) and its null result is more trustworthy.
Expressed relative to the typical between-population difference for the focal species, both estimates are extremely imprecise (Ruficollis vs. Hypoxantha: -0.780, 95% CI [-5.768, 0.874]; Hypoxantha vs. Ruficollis: 0.005, 95% CI [-6.764, 4.826]) — the data cannot rule out a shift as large as several ordinary population differences in either direction.



Interpretation

With only one species pair testable and very few populations per comparison, Step 3 has essentially no statistical power for simple songs: the absence of a credible shift reflects data scarcity more than evidence against population-level convergence or divergence.
The point estimates are at least directionally consistent with the Step 2 sympatry pattern: Ruficollis populations that co-occur with Hypoxantha trend towards acoustic convergence (negative shift) rather than divergence, the opposite of what simple-song character displacement in Step 2 would predict if it operated through this specific species’ shift; given the width of the interval, however, this is only a weak hint and not a finding.

title: Step 3: Population shifts towards or away from congeners
text:
Summary

Model summary

As for simple songs, only Ruficollis vs. Hypoxantha and Hypoxantha vs. Ruficollis are testable. Neither co-occurrence effect is credible (Ruficollis vs. Hypoxantha: -0.346 SD, 95% CI [-0.980, 0.516]; Hypoxantha vs. Ruficollis: 0.052 SD, 95% CI [-0.537, 0.576]), and both models converged cleanly (Rhat = 1, divergent transitions below 1% in both).
Relative to the typical between-population difference, both estimates are again extremely imprecise (Ruficollis vs. Hypoxantha: -1.450, 95% CI [-51.529, 0.908]; Hypoxantha vs. Ruficollis: 0.379, 95% CI [-4.070, 18.238]).



Interpretation

As with simple songs, Step 3 provides no credible evidence of population-level convergence or divergence for complex songs, but this is a statement about statistical power (one testable species pair, few populations) rather than about biology.
Unlike the simple-song Hypoxantha vs. Ruficollis model, both complex-song models converged cleanly, so these null results are not undermined by sampling problems — they are genuinely uninformative given the data available, not masked by a convergence failure.
Taken together with Step 2, the strongest and best-supported evidence for sound-based character displacement in this system remains the heterospecific sympatric-vs-allopatric contrast (Step 2), not the population-shift framing used here, which is limited by how few species pairs have the co-occurrence structure needed to test it.

Do songs vary across each species’ range, and is that variation organized by population? Here we compare songs of different individuals of the same species recorded in the same population with those recorded in different populations. If songs are population-structured, within-population pairs should be more similar (smaller acoustic distance) than between-population pairs. This also shows that there is local variation on which sympatry could act (Step 3).
Acoustic distance is the same PCA-based Euclidean distance used in the sympatry models. Pairs of songs from the same individual are excluded.

title: Step 1: Population structure within species
text:
1.1 Model: within vs. between populations
\[
\begin{split}
\text{acoustic distance} &\sim \text{species} + \text{species} : \text{same population} \\
&\quad + (1 \mid \text{mm(population}_1,\text{population}_2)) \\
&\quad + (1 \mid \text{mm(individual}_1,\text{individual}_2))
\end{split}
\]

Only conspecific pairs from species sampled in more than one population.
species:same_population1 is the species-specific difference in acoustic distance between within- and between-population pairs. Negative values mean songs are more similar within populations.
Species enter as fixed effects because only two species have more than one population. The intercept is the baseline (between-population) distance of the reference species and species is the baseline difference of the other species. This parameterization keeps the regularizing prior on the effects and the baseline difference only, not on species means.
Multi-membership random effects for population and individual, as in the sympatry models.
The response is standardized within the model dataset (both species pooled), so effects are in SD units. Regularizing priors as in the trait-level sympatry models: normal(0, 1) for the intercept, normal(0, 0.5) for fixed effects, exponential(2) for random-effect SDs (including the multi-membership terms) and exponential(1) for the residual SD.

title: Step 1: Population structure within species
text:
Summary

Model summary

Within-population pairs are credibly more similar than between-population pairs for Hypoxantha (species:same_population1 = -0.164 SD, 95% CI [-0.197, -0.131]) and, more strongly, for Ruficollis (-0.463 SD, 95% CI [-0.496, -0.430]) — roughly a three-fold larger effect. Both models converged cleanly (Rhat = 1, no credible-interval-crossing issues).
The isolation-by-distance slope is not credible for Hypoxantha (-0.267 SD, 95% CI [-1.160, 0.631]) but is credible and negative for Ruficollis (-0.366 SD, 95% CI [-0.435, -0.295]). With only 3-6 independent population pairs per species, this estimate is informed by very little independent replication and should be read as descriptive.



Interpretation

Simple songs carry genuine, population-level geographic structure in both species with more than one population, confirming there is local song variation for sympatry to act on in Step 3.
The much stronger structuring in Ruficollis suggests either more restricted song learning/dispersal or more time for populations to diverge in that species than in Hypoxantha.
The negative, rather than positive, isolation-by-distance trend in Ruficollis indicates that this population structure is not simply accumulating with geographic distance as under neutral drift — distant populations are not more acoustically different than nearby ones. This is consistent with song divergence being driven by local factors (habitat acoustics, drift in small founder populations, or selective pressures such as sympatry with congeners) rather than by isolation by distance per se, though the small number of population pairs means this should be treated as a hypothesis for the sympatry-focused steps rather than a confirmed result.

title: Step 1: Population structure within species
text:
Summary

Model summary

The within- vs. between-population effect is not credible for Hypoxantha (0.019 SD, 95% CI [-0.028, 0.065], overlapping zero and even slightly positive in direction) and is credible but smaller than in simple songs for Ruficollis (-0.267 SD, 95% CI [-0.371, -0.165]).

Interpretation

Unlike simple songs, complex songs carry little to no detectable population-level geographic signal in Hypoxantha, and a weaker signal than simple songs in Ruficollis.
This asymmetry suggests complex songs are more stereotyped/conserved across each species’ range — plausibly because they are under stronger stabilizing selection (e.g., species or mate recognition), are more constrained by shared motor templates, or are simply noisier measurements given fewer recordings per population.
Practically, Step 3’s test for sympatry-driven shifts has much less population-level variation to work with for complex songs than for simple songs, so any sympatry effect detected later for complex songs is acting on a flatter geographic baseline.

title: Vocal character displacement in southern capuchinos
text: This site contains the analyses of vocal character displacement in southern capuchino seedeaters (Sporophila spp.). We evaluate whether songs of different species are more or less divergent where they co-occur, how much each species’ song varies across its range, and which species’ populations shifted where they live with congeners.

title: Vocal character displacement in southern capuchinos
text:
Analysis reports
The analysis starts with a data preparation report (PCA and pairwise acoustic distances for simple and complex songs), followed by three analysis steps, each run separately for simple and complex songs:

Population structure within species. Are songs of individuals from the same population more similar than songs from different populations, beyond isolation by distance? This shows there is local variation on which sympatry could act. It can only be tested for species sampled in more than one population (hypoxantha and ruficollis); the other species are described.
Sympatry and heterospecific distances. Are heterospecific songs more or less different in sympatry than in allopatry (the sympatry-only models)? A dyadic comparison cannot show which species changed.
Population shifts. Within a focal species, are populations that co-occur with a congener shifted towards (convergence) or away from (divergence) that congener’s song, compared with conspecific populations that do not co-occur with it?

Step 3 can only be tested for hypoxantha and ruficollis relative to each other, because iberaensis and palustris were recorded at a single locality. It rests on very few populations per contrast (2 vs. 2 for ruficollis, 1 vs. 2 for hypoxantha), and single-site contrasts are confounded with anything else particular to that locality. It is therefore presented as supporting evidence, and the size of any co-occurrence shift is compared with ordinary between-population differences.

title: Vocal character displacement in southern capuchinos
text:
Main results

Population structure (Step 1). Simple songs are population-structured in both testable species, more strongly in Ruficollis than in Hypoxantha. Complex songs show little to no structuring in Hypoxantha and weaker structuring than simple songs in Ruficollis. Neither song type shows a clear isolation-by-distance signal, so this local structure is not simply accumulating with geographic distance.
Sympatry (Step 2). Simple heterospecific songs are credibly more divergent in sympatry than in allopatry, and consistently so across all three testable species pairs — the pattern predicted by sound-based character displacement. Complex songs show the same direction of effect but far weaker overall, driven mainly by one species pair (Hypoxantha-Palustris); at the trait level, complex-song divergence in sympatry is a mosaic, with element-level acoustic distance, gap duration, frequency range and element diversity increasing in sympatry while peak frequency and song rate actually converge.
Population shifts (Step 3). No credible population-level shifts (convergence or divergence) were detected for either song type. Only one species pair (Hypoxantha vs. Ruficollis) has enough co-occurrence structure to test, so this null result reflects very limited statistical power rather than evidence against a shift.
Overall, the clearest and best-supported evidence for character displacement in this system is the simple-song sympatry effect in Step 2; complex songs and the population-shift framing provide weaker, more qualified support.

    FUN = function(x) {

        selected_sorted <- cumprop <= 0.5  # variables with 50% of contribution

        selected <- logical(length(x))

# element_markdown() below, parses these labels as markdown-with-HTML; an

# that parser and silently fail to render the whole plot)
escape_markdown <- function(x) {

  x <- gsub(">", ">", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("_", "_", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("*", "*", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x

pca_rot_stck$label_col <- ifelse(
  pca_rot_stck$stable,
  paste0("<span style='color:black;'>", escape_markdown(pca_rot_stck$variable), "</span>"),
  paste0("<span style='color:gray50;'>", escape_markdown(pca_rot_stck$variable), "</span>")

# passed the whole top_vars column as "values" to scale_alpha_manual, which
# expects one value per factor level, not per row - fragile even before the

    scale_x_discrete(labels = label_vec, name = "Variable") +

Summary

Model summary

Element-level PCA on simple songs retained 4 PCs (broken-stick criterion), explaining 78.8% of acoustic variance.
Song-level features were more redundant: song duration correlated strongly with both song rate (r = -0.80) and number of elements (r = 0.78), and frequency range with element diversity/mst (r = 0.80), so the song-level PCA collapsed to a single broken-stick PC explaining only 47.6% of variance.



Interpretation

Simple-song element structure is multidimensional — four largely independent axes of spectro-temporal variation are needed to summarize it — whereas the song-level description is effectively one-dimensional, dominated by a timing/pace axis (duration, rate and number of elements move together).
The element-level PCA distance therefore carries most of the fine-grained acoustic information for simple songs, while the single song-level PC mainly captures how fast/long a song is rather than independent facets of structure; downstream models based on element-level distance should be more sensitive to subtle divergence than those based on the single song-level PC.

pca_rot_stck <- stack(pca_rot)

pca_rot_stck$variable <- rownames(pca_rot)

    "PC1"]
pca_rot_stck$Sign <- ifelse(pca_rot_stck$values > 0, "Positive", "Negative")
pca_rot_stck$rotation <- abs(pca_rot_stck$values)
pca_rot_stck$ind_var <- paste0(pca_rot_stck$ind, " (", sapply(pca_rot_stck$ind,
    function(x) pca_var[names(pca_var) == x]), "%)")

pca_rot_stck$top_vars <- ave(abs(pca_rot_stck$values), pca_rot_stck$ind,
    FUN = function(x) {

        # Order decreasing
        ord <- order(x, decreasing = TRUE)
        x_sorted <- x[ord]

        # Cumulative proportion
        cumprop <- cumsum(x_sorted)/sum(x_sorted)

        selected_sorted <- cumprop <= 0.5  # variables with 50% of contribution
        selected_sorted[which(cumprop >= 0.5)[1]] <- TRUE

        # Return logical vector in original order
        selected <- logical(length(x))
        selected[ord] <- selected_sorted

        selected
    })

# Create facet-specific variable

    sep = "_")

    }))

    freq_threshold = 0.5, seed = 123)

    "ind"), all.x = TRUE)

# rather than letting NA propagate into the plot aesthetics below
pca_rot_stck$stable[is.na(pca_rot_stck$stable)] <- FALSE

# Build colored labels per row

# escape characters that markdown/HTML treats specially (gridtext, used by
# element_markdown() below, parses these labels as markdown-with-HTML; an
# unescaped &, <, > or an odd number of _ / * in a variable name can break
# that parser and silently fail to render the whole plot)
escape_markdown <- function(x) {
  x <- gsub("&", "&", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("<", "<", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub(">", ">", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("_", "_", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("*", "*", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x
}

# Colored labels: black for stable variables, gray for the rest
# (previously compared stable < 1.1, which is true whether stable is 0 or
# 1, so every label always took the black branch)
pca_rot_stck$label_col <- ifelse(
  pca_rot_stck$stable,
  paste0("<span style='color:black;'>", escape_markdown(pca_rot_stck$variable), "</span>"),
  paste0("<span style='color:gray50;'>", escape_markdown(pca_rot_stck$variable), "</span>")

# Named vector for labels

# absolute CI

pca_rot_stck$ci_high_plot <- abs(pca_rot_stck$ci_upper)

# Plot
# alpha is used directly as a numeric value (scale_alpha_identity) rather
# than mapped through as.factor()/scale_alpha_manual(); the previous version
# passed the whole top_vars column as "values" to scale_alpha_manual, which
# expects one value per factor level, not per row - fragile even before the
# always-1 bug above was fixed
ggplot(pca_rot_stck, aes(x = var_facet, y = rotation, fill = Sign,
    alpha = top_vars)) + geom_col() + coord_flip() + scale_alpha_identity(guide = NULL) +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = label_vec, name = "Variable") +
    labs(x = "Rotation") + scale_fill_viridis_d(alpha = 0.7, begin = 0.2,

    theme(axis.text.y = element_markdown())

Model summary

Complex-song element-level PCA retained 5 PCs explaining 81.5% of variance (vs. 4 PCs/78.8% for simple songs), and the song-level PCA retained 2 PCs explaining 73.7% of variance (vs. 1 PC/47.6% for simple songs).
Song-level features were again highly collinear, most strikingly number of elements with song duration (r = 0.96) and with element diversity/mst (r = 0.83).



Interpretation

Complex songs need more PCs to summarize both their elements and their overall structure, consistent with them being acoustically richer/more variable than simple songs.
Unlike simple songs, the complex song-level description is not reducible to a single timing axis — a second, largely independent PC is needed — but the very high correlation between number of elements and song duration indicates complex songs are still built by lengthening songs mainly by adding elements rather than by varying element pacing.
These differences matter for comparing the simple- and complex-song results in later steps: the complex-song PCA-based distance integrates more independent acoustic information than the simple-song one, and the single most problematic redundancy (elements/duration) should be interpreted as one signal, not two, wherever both appear among the significant per-feature results.

title: Step 2: Sympatry and heterospecific distances
text:
1.1 Statistical analysis
To evaluate whether acoustic divergence between heterospecific songs differed between sympatric and allopatric population comparisons, we fitted a Bayesian mixed-effects model while accounting for the non-independence inherent to pairwise distance data.
The model was specified as:
\[
\begin{split}
\text{acoustic distance} &\sim \text{sympatry} \\
&\quad + (1 \mid \text{species pair}) \\
&\quad + (1 \mid \text{mm(population}_1,\text{population}_2)) \\
&\quad + (1 \mid \text{mm(individual}_1,\text{individual}_2))
\end{split}
\]
where:

(_{ij}) is the Euclidean distance between songs (i) and (j) in multivariate acoustic space.
(_{ij}) is a binary predictor indicating whether the populations from which songs (i) and (j) were recorded occur in sympatry (1) or allopatry (0).
species pair is a random intercept accounting for baseline differences in acoustic divergence among heterospecific species combinations.
mm(population(_1), population(_2)) is a multi-membership random effect accounting for repeated use of the same populations across pairwise comparisons.
mm(individual(_1), individual(_2)) is a multi-membership random effect accounting for repeated use of the same individuals across pairwise comparisons.

Model specifications:

The model was fitted in a Bayesian framework using the brms package, with sympatry as the only fixed effect. Geographic distance was not included: sympatric comparisons are all within-locality and allopatric comparisons all between localities, so sympatry and geographic distance cannot be separated with this sampling (posterior correlation between their coefficients of about 0.9 in the models that included both). Because isolation by distance predicts greater similarity at short distances, omitting geographic distance should, if anything, make the sympatry effect conservative when acoustic distance increases with geographic distance.
The response variable was pairwise Euclidean acoustic distance and was modeled using a Gaussian error distribution.
Only heterospecific comparisons were included.
Analyses were restricted to species pairs for which both sympatric and allopatric population comparisons were available. This restriction ensured that sympatry effects were estimated within the same species-pair contrasts rather than being confounded by species pairs occurring exclusively in sympatry or exclusively in allopatry.
Species-pair identity was included as a random intercept to account for inherent differences in acoustic divergence among species combinations.
Population identity was modeled using a multi-membership random effect because each pairwise comparison simultaneously involves two populations, and each population contributes to multiple pairwise distances.
Individual identity was modeled using a multi-membership random effect because each pairwise comparison simultaneously involves two individuals, and each individual contributes to multiple pairwise distances.
Only unique pairwise comparisons were retained and self-comparisons were excluded.
Weakly informative, regularizing priors were specified for all parameters.
The model was fitted using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo as implemented in Stan through the cmdstanr backend.

The coefficient for sympatry in this model represents the difference in acoustic divergence between sympatric (within-locality) and allopatric (between-locality) heterospecific comparisons, after accounting for the hierarchical structure of the data. The same model structure was fitted separately for the overall PCA-based acoustic distance and for each individual acoustic feature, so that trait-specific effects of sympatry could be examined alongside the overall pattern.

Summary

Model summary

Sympatric heterospecific pairs have credibly greater PCA-based acoustic distance than allopatric pairs (sympatry1 = 0.227 SD, 95% CI [0.204, 0.250]), with clean convergence (Rhat = 1, no CIs near zero).
The model produced divergent transitions (858/20,000 draws, 4.3%), concentrated in the species-pair random-effect SD (estimated from only 3 levels) rather than spread across chains. The sympatry coefficient is essentially identical in divergent and non-divergent draws (median 0.236 vs. 0.227, overlapping 95% ranges), so the divergences reflect a weakly identified variance component and do not bias the effect of interest.



Interpretation

Simple songs of heterospecific pairs are more acoustically different where the species co-occur than where they do not — the signature predicted by sound-based character displacement (selection against acoustic confusion in sympatry, e.g. via reproductive interference or mistaken aggression).
As detailed in the species-pair breakdown below, this pattern is not an artifact of one species pair dominating the pooled estimate: all three heterospecific pairs individually show a credible positive sympatry effect, though its magnitude differs between pairs.




1.1.1.1.6 Contrasts by species pair
The model above estimates a single sympatry effect for all species pairs; species pair enters only as a varying intercept, which shifts sympatric and allopatric comparisons by the same amount and therefore cannot tell whether the effect is shared by all pairs or driven by one of them. To obtain a separate sympatry effect for each species pair, the model is refitted with species-pair-specific sympatry slopes (a varying slope of sympatry by species pair, correlated with the varying intercept, with an LKJ(2) prior on the correlation). The per-pair effect is the fixed sympatry effect plus the pair’s deviation; the pairwise differences between species pairs are computed from the posterior draws. With only three species pairs the between-pair standard deviation of the sympatry slope, and its correlation with the intercept, are weakly informed by the data and lean on the priors; the per-pair effects are partially pooled towards the overall effect, so they should be read as shrunken estimates rather than as three independent fits. The fitting chunk is not evaluated when rendering (it takes as long as the main model); run it once and the results are loaded from the saved fit.

title: Step 2: Sympatry and heterospecific distances
text:
2.1 Statistical analysis
To evaluate whether acoustic divergence between heterospecific songs differed between sympatric and allopatric population comparisons, we fitted a Bayesian mixed-effects model while accounting for the non-independence inherent to pairwise distance data.
The model was specified as:
\[
\begin{split}
\text{acoustic distance} &\sim \text{sympatry} \\
&\quad + (1 \mid \text{species pair}) \\
&\quad + (1 \mid \text{mm(population}_1,\text{population}_2)) \\
&\quad + (1 \mid \text{mm(individual}_1,\text{individual}_2))
\end{split}
\]
where:

(_{ij}) is the Euclidean distance between songs (i) and (j) in multivariate acoustic space.
(_{ij}) is a binary predictor indicating whether the populations from which songs (i) and (j) were recorded occur in sympatry (1) or allopatry (0).
species pair is a random intercept accounting for baseline differences in acoustic divergence among heterospecific species combinations.
mm(population(_1), population(_2)) is a multi-membership random effect accounting for repeated use of the same populations across pairwise comparisons.
mm(individual(_1), individual(_2)) is a multi-membership random effect accounting for repeated use of the same individuals across pairwise comparisons.

Model specifications:

The model was fitted in a Bayesian framework using the brms package, with sympatry as the only fixed effect. Geographic distance was not included: sympatric comparisons are all within-locality and allopatric comparisons all between localities, so sympatry and geographic distance cannot be separated with this sampling (posterior correlation between their coefficients of about 0.9 in the models that included both). Because isolation by distance predicts greater similarity at short distances, omitting geographic distance should, if anything, make the sympatry effect conservative when acoustic distance increases with geographic distance.
The response variable was pairwise Euclidean acoustic distance and was modeled using a Gaussian error distribution.
Only heterospecific comparisons were included.
Analyses were restricted to species pairs for which both sympatric and allopatric population comparisons were available. This restriction ensured that sympatry effects were estimated within the same species-pair contrasts rather than being confounded by species pairs occurring exclusively in sympatry or exclusively in allopatry.
Species-pair identity was included as a random intercept to account for inherent differences in acoustic divergence among species combinations.
Population identity was modeled using a multi-membership random effect because each pairwise comparison simultaneously involves two populations, and each population contributes to multiple pairwise distances.
Individual identity was modeled using a multi-membership random effect because each pairwise comparison simultaneously involves two individuals, and each individual contributes to multiple pairwise distances.
Only unique pairwise comparisons were retained and self-comparisons were excluded.
Weakly informative, regularizing priors were specified for all parameters.
The model was fitted using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo as implemented in Stan through the cmdstanr backend.

The coefficient for sympatry in this model represents the difference in acoustic divergence between sympatric (within-locality) and allopatric (between-locality) heterospecific comparisons, after accounting for the hierarchical structure of the data. The same model structure was fitted separately for the overall PCA-based acoustic distance and for each individual acoustic feature, so that trait-specific effects of sympatry could be examined alongside the overall pattern.

2.1.1 Model fitting

2.1.1.1 PCA-based acoustic distance
Prepare data for modeling by restricting to species pairs with both sympatric and allopatric comparisons and creating appropriate random effect structures.

  sympatric <- intersect(pops1, pops2)

  if(length(sympatric) == 0) {
    sympatric_txt <- "none"
  } else {
    sympatric_txt <- paste(sympatric, collapse = ", ")
  }

  allopatric <- setdiff(union(pops1, pops2), sympatric)

  if(length(allopatric) == 0) {
    allopatric_txt <- "none"
  } else {
    allopatric_txt <- paste(allopatric, collapse = ", ")
  }

  results <- rbind(
    results,

2.1.1.1.5 Divergent transitions
The sampler produced divergent transitions in this model. Divergences mark regions of the posterior that Hamiltonian Monte Carlo could not explore reliably, so estimates from those regions may be biased (Betancourt 2017). Without refitting, the checks below show (1) how many post-warmup draws diverged and whether they are concentrated in one chain, (2) whether divergences pile up at small values of any random-effect SD (a “funnel”; the species-pair SD, estimated from only three levels, is the most likely candidate), and (3) whether the fixed-effect estimates differ between divergent and non-divergent draws. If divergences are confined to a random-effect SD and the fixed effects look the same in both sets of draws, the inference on sympatry is unlikely to be affected. These checks cannot show what the sampler failed to explore, so refitting (e.g. with species pair as a fixed effect) remains the definitive test.

Sympatric pairs have credibly greater PCA-based acoustic distance than allopatric pairs (sympatry1 = 0.042 SD, 95% CI [0.009, 0.076]), but the effect is roughly 5-fold smaller than for simple songs (0.227 SD) and its CI sits close to zero.

Interpretation

Complex songs show the same qualitative sign of character displacement as simple songs (greater divergence in sympatry) but a much weaker pooled signal.
The species-pair breakdown below shows this weak pooled effect is driven almost entirely by one pair (Hypoxantha-Palustris); the other two heterospecific pairs show no credible sympatry effect for complex songs, unlike simple songs where all three pairs diverged credibly. 2.1.1.1.6 Contrasts by species pair
The model above estimates a single sympatry effect for all species pairs; species pair enters only as a varying intercept, which shifts sympatric and allopatric comparisons by the same amount and therefore cannot tell whether the effect is shared by all pairs or driven by one of them. To obtain a separate sympatry effect for each species pair, the model is refitted with species-pair-specific sympatry slopes (a varying slope of sympatry by species pair, correlated with the varying intercept, with an LKJ(2) prior on the correlation). The per-pair effect is the fixed sympatry effect plus the pair’s deviation; the pairwise differences between species pairs are computed from the posterior draws. With only three species pairs the between-pair standard deviation of the sympatry slope, and its correlation with the intercept, are weakly informed by the data and lean on the priors; the per-pair effects are partially pooled towards the overall effect, so they should be read as shrunken estimates rather than as three independent fits.   rm(fit)
  invisible(gc(verbose = FALSE))
}

Summary

Model summary

Of the 8 trait-level models, 6 have credible sympatry effects. Element-level PCA distance shows by far the largest effect (1.279 SD, 95% CI [1.252, 1.306]) — an order of magnitude larger than any single song-level feature. Among song-level features, frequency range (0.038, 95% CI [0.001, 0.075]), gap duration (0.063, 95% CI [0.030, 0.097]) and element diversity/mst (0.044, 95% CI [0.010, 0.078]) are credibly positive (greater distance in sympatry), while peak frequency (-0.063, 95% CI [-0.097, -0.029]) and song rate (-0.082, 95% CI [-0.116, -0.049]) are credibly negative (smaller distance in sympatry). Number of elements (0.000) and song duration (0.005) show no credible effect.
Divergent transitions stayed below 2% for every feature, and the sympatry coefficient is essentially unchanged between divergent and non-divergent draws in every model, so none of these conclusions hinge on the divergences.



Interpretation

The character-displacement signal in complex songs is concentrated at the fine-grained element level: element-level acoustic distance is massively amplified in sympatry, far beyond what the overall song-level PCA-based model (0.042 SD) or any single song-level feature shows. Averaging element-level detail into song-level descriptors appears to dilute a strong underlying signal.
Song-level features show a mosaic rather than uniform divergence: gap duration, frequency range and element diversity/mst diverge modestly in sympatry (consistent with selection against acoustic confusion), but peak frequency and song rate actually converge in sympatry — heterospecific pairs sound more alike in pace and dominant frequency where they co-occur than where they do not.
This convergence in frequency and rate is the opposite of classical character displacement and is more consistent with shared ecological/acoustic constraints in sympatry (e.g. adaptation to the same habitat acoustics, morphological convergence in body size, or selection on these particular features for interspecific territorial signalling) acting alongside divergence in other traits. Complex-song divergence in sympatry is therefore trait-specific rather than a wholesale shift of the song.
